overview: The Aghlabids governed Ifriqiya, centred on Kairouan in present-day Tunisia, while acknowledging the Abbasid caliph. Their court, towns and Mediterranean connections supported distinctive architecture, craftsmanship and learning.

periods.title: An autonomous ruling dynasty
periods.summary: Harun al-Rashid appointed Ibrahim al-Aghlab hereditary emir in 800. His dynasty appointed officials and minted coins while acknowledging Baghdad’s sovereignty.

periods.title: Rebuilding Kairouan’s Great Mosque
periods.summary: Ziyadat Allah I rebuilt the Great Mosque in 836 on an older religious site. Its monumental form was further enriched by later Aghlabid work.

periods.title: Public waterworks and urban life
periods.summary: Reservoirs built between 860 and 862 collected, settled and stored water for Kairouan. They supported residents, caravans and livestock during shortages.

periods.title: After Aghlabid rule
periods.summary: Fatimid conquest ended the emirate in 909. The map’s later coverage reflects coarse snapshots, not continued Aghlabid government.

items.text: Kairouan’s reservoirs receive runoff and water from tributaries of the Merguellil valley. Water first enters a settling basin, then passes through an outlet into a larger storage basin and covered cisterns. The sequence separates sediment removal from storage and drawing, showing how the builders organized a practical response to unreliable rainfall.

Rubble masonry, thick plaster and buttresses helped the basins retain water and withstand its pressure. The heritage account explains their use for people facing shortages, including poorer residents, as well as caravans and livestock. Public storage supplemented household wells and cisterns rather than replacing every private supply.

sections.title: Architecture and the work of skilled makers

items.text: The Great Mosque’s pillared prayer hall reuses Roman and Byzantine columns and capitals. New arrangements brought older building materials into an Islamic place of worship. A fluted dome and carved supports emphasize the area before the mihrab, showing that reuse and new design were combined rather than being separate architectural choices.

The mihrab combines carved marble, painted wood and lustre-glazed ceramic tiles. These different surfaces create a layered setting for prayer. The catalogue links the ninth-century tiles with Iraq; the building also contains later restorations, so not every surviving feature should be attributed to Aghlabid builders.

Raqqada museum’s teak fragment BS 200 came from the Great Mosque’s minbar, the preacher’s pulpit. Its carved vine leaves and grape clusters belonged to the stair’s upper edge. Joining separately carved components produced an elaborate furnishing whose craftsmanship served the weekly act of public preaching.

The fragment is dated through historical accounts and comparison with other ninth-century decoration. Its workshop remains debated: references to Baghdad do not settle where it was carved. Removal during restoration around 1920 explains how this component entered the museum record; it was not excavated from Raqqada’s palaces.

Bowl C 34, recovered at Raqqada, combines green, brown and yellow glaze with repeated kufic lettering for al-Mulk, or sovereignty. Its surface shows how calligraphy could become part of vessel decoration. The catalogue associates the colours with copper, manganese and antimony or iron compounds, connecting the appearance to material choices.

The bowl is usually assigned to the late ninth-century Aghlabid repertoire, but its 1960s excavation lacked a detailed record. Similar forms and techniques continued under the Fatimids. Style therefore supports an approximate attribution, while the missing archaeological context prevents a securely dated manufacturing year.

Gold dinar M 200 carries the date 192 AH, rendered by the museum as 808 CE. Its kufic inscriptions include the dynastic emblem ghalaba within a layout related to Abbasid coinage. Unlike a vessel dated mainly by style, this coin contains direct written evidence for its issue date.

The museum attributes the dinar to Kairouan and describes Aghlabid gold coinage circulating in Mediterranean commerce. That connects a small object with government and exchange. The catalogue does not provide this specimen’s excavation findspot, so its present museum location cannot reconstruct a particular merchant’s route.
Sahnun’s compilation of Maliki teachings in the Mudawwana became a major reference for North African law. Kairouan’s scholarship was an achievement alongside its buildings and objects.

Farmers and artisans supplied grain, olive oil and textiles to exchange networks. Those networks also trafficked enslaved people across the Mediterranean and Sahara. Prosperity depended on unequal relationships as well as productive work.

ending.text: The Fatimids conquered Aghlabid Ifriqiya in 909, ending the dynasty’s rule. Local building practices and infrastructure continued under the new rulers. The map has no Fatimid geometry at 909, so a successor link would give a misleading location for the event.
